A HISTORY OF THE UPSILON CHAPTER OF
THE PSI UPSILON FRATERNITY.
BY GEOBGE A. COE, '84.
Ee.id at the twenty-fifth anniversary ot the founding of the
Chapter, February 12, 1883.
CHAPTEE I.
BFFOETS TO OBTAIN A OHABTEE.
�
One of the most interesting periods in the life of a
married coupb is that in which the courtship takes
place. As we have assembled to celebrate the mar
riage of a certain Eochester party with the coy maiden
Psi Upsilon, it will not be out of place to recall the
courtship of that worthy couple. The story cannot
fail to be interesting, for this maiden was not easily
won. Longfellow's lines might almost be applied to
Psi Upsilon :
"
I know a maiden fair to see,
Take care !
She can both false and friendly be,
Beware! Beware!
Trust her not,
She is fooling thee !"
To find the very beginning of the Upsilon's his
tory, we must go back, not twenty-five, but thirty
years. The project of having a Chapter of Psi U. in
the University of Eochester was conceived about five
years before it met with success. The University was
then in its infancy, having been in operation only
three years. It occupied a building on West Main
(then Buffalo) street, which had formerly been used
as a hotel. The hotel dining room had been meta
morphosed into a chapsl. Above the chapel and
lecture rooms were several apartments which served
as a small dormitory. The old University is still
standing. It is the second building east of the Erie
canal, on the north side of West Main street. It is a
four-story brick block painted a sort of drab. The
ground floor is occupied by various stores, and the
upper stories are used as dwellings. The ancient
character of the building is indicated by two small
pillars in relief, which stand at the sides of the main
entrance. The grimy old block has no suggestion of
classical associations about it, yet it possesses, for
the Eochester man, quite a little historic interest.
At the time of which we speak, our venerable and
beloved President Anderson was in the prime of life,
and had just been elected to the oflce which he has
so long and honorably filled. The Chapters of Alpha
Delta Phi, Delta Psi, and Delta Upsilon (formerly
called the Equitable Society), were already organized.
Psi Upsilon had eleven Chapters, the Alpha being
the yonngest.
Such was the condition of things when the question
of having a Chapter of Psi U. in Eochester was flrst
agitated. The honor of fathering this idea must be
accorded to Dr. John C. Overhiser of New York.
This brother matriculated at the University of the
City of New York, entering the class of 1854, and be
came a member of the Delta Chapter of Psi U. After
finishing his Junior year, he entered the University
of Eochester, and graduated in 1854. During his
stay in this city, it occurred to him that there ought
to be a Chapter of his Fraternity here. This desire
was strengthened by the course then pursued by
Alpha Delta Phi, which, he says,
"
in the early his
tory of the University,
"
ruled things with a high
hand." Bro. Overhiser communicated his idea to
several other students, and the result was the forma
tion of a local society, whose principal object was
opposition to Alpha Delt., but which also had in view
the establishment of a Psi U. Chapter. Promineutly
associated with Bro. Overhiser in organizing this

4 THE DIAMOND.
movement were Eandolph C. Brant, '54 ; Galusba
Anderson, '54, now President of the University of
Chicago ; and A. J. Barrett, '54. of this city. All of
these gentlemen graduated before the Upsilon was
organized, and only one, Bro. Barrett, ever became a
member of the Fraternity.
The founders of this society were, with one excep
tion, in favor of having a
Chapter of Psi U. here.
The exception was Galusha Anderson, who had been
soured on tlje subject of secret societies by some
trouble he had had with the Delta Psi's. *
This organization was christened the Innominata
Society, and its name was soon permitted to appear
with those of other societies in the University. The
Innominata seems to have become popular immedi
ately, for it began its career with a membership of
about twenty of the best men in the University.
Although the Innominata was not, as we shall see
hereafter, strictly speaking, the origin of the Upsilon,
yet it rendered material aid in the formation of that
Chapter. It was John the Baptist preparing the
way for him who was to come. It kept alive the
idea of having a Psi U. Chapter in Eochester, and
prevented several of those who became the founders
of the Upsilon from joining any of the Fraternities
then in operation. It rushed men just as the other
societies did, and held out the inducement of possible
future membership in Psi U. To show the relition
of the Innominata to the Upsilon, I will tell you how
two of our early members became Psi U's. Dr. Chas.
A. Dewey, '61, was rushed for Psi U. by his tutor,
who was a member of the Innominata. Bro. Barrett,
'54, after graduating became Principal of the Nunda
Literary Institute, where he did the future Upsilon a
'
good service by rushing the sub-fresh for the Innom
inata. John P. Colby, '59, was thus induced to join
that society, and became one of the charter members
of the Upsilon.
The Innominata occupied roorbs on the east side of
State street, probably in the building which still
stands on the south corner of Market street. Its
meetings were of a
literary character, and were con
ducted somewhat like those of the Fraternity Chap
ters. I have not been able to find any traces of the
records of this old organizaticni. It would be a
piece
of good fortune if they could be found and put into
the possession of the Chapter.
It is probable that a petition for a new
Chapter was
sent to the Convention of 1854, but, as I have not had
access to the records of Conventions prior to 1857, I
have not yet been able to ascertain the exact truth.
The Delta Kappa Epsilon established a
Chapter
here in 1856. The men who organized it first applied
to our Convention for a
charter, and, being refused,
turned to zi. K. E., where they were successful. One
*
We have an interesting document relating to this affair
among our archives. <^^mi;
who remembers the circumstances understands that
our Convention denied their petition
"
because of
their promiscuousness," or
something of that sort. A
letter from Bro. Colby of St. Louis, shows how the
Convention received its information. He says :
' '
I have heard of unsuccessful applications. * *
One of these was by a junto of the boys of our time,
who finally decided that Psi U. grapes were
probably sour, and that nothing was quite so
nicely
suited to their taste as crab-apples of the A. K. E.
variety. It has sometimes occurred to me that their
preference for crab-apples might be largely due to a
confidential correspondenoe which sprung up, while
their application was
pending, between the subscriber
and Wm. P. Warner (our old townsman), of the &.
Chapter. Indeed, the latter has, ou more than one
occasion, admitted his share of this rather grave re
sponsibility, and, instead of being depressed with its
consideration, he seemed to find in it a deep source
of satisfaction.
"
I have said that the Innominata kept alive the idea
of having a
Chapter of Psi Upsilon in Eochester.
Several circumstances united to prevent this society,
as a
body, becoming a
Chapter of our
Fraternity.
The hostility which existed originally toward the
Alpha Delts seems to have developed finally into
opposition to secret societies in general, at least, on
the part of some of the Innoms. Moreover, some
persons had gained admission to this society who
were not considered specially ornamental to it, and
those members who were
ssekiug admission to Psi U.
did not desire to be encumbered by poor men. The
question of turning the society over to Psi U. was
discussed informally, and considerable opposition was
manifested. No formal action, however, was taken.
Finally, John P. Colby, '59, Ira C. Clark, '59, and
George W. Houghton, '59, resigned from the Innom
inata, for the purpose of organizing a new
society,
Psi U. if possible.
An application for a charter was now drawn up and
sent to the Convention. of 1857. It was signed by
eight persons, whose names are as follows : Egbert
Hurd, '58, H. L. Morehouse, '58, Ira C. Clark, '59,'
J. P. Colby, '59, .Joshua Gaskill, '5y, E. P. Gould,
'59, G. W. Houghton, '59, F. A. Williams, '60. All
of the petitioners, excepting Bros. Hurd and More
house, had been members of the Innominata, which
fact shows a
pretty close . connection between that
society and the Upsilon. Bro. Morehouse performed
much of the clerical labor in procuring the Chapter.
This petition was favored by resident Psi U's, espe
cially Bros. A. H. Strong, B., '57, and Theodore
Bacon, B., '53. The Beta championed the cause in
the Convention.
In the record of the Convention of this year, 1857,
it is stated that :
"
On motion of Bro. Middleton (B.),
the application from the University of Eochester, N.

THE DIAMOND. 5
for the establishment of a Chapter, was referred
to the Committee on New Chapters."
A similar application from the University of North
Carolina was also referred to the Committee on New
Chapters. A little further on in the record occurs
this passage :
"The following Eeport was presented by Bro.
Cobb (P.), Chairman of Committee on New Chap
ters, which was accepted :
" '
We have considered the different applications
made for the establisment of new Chapters. The one
presented by Bro. Hall (2.), coming from North Car
olina University, we do not regard with favor. The
fact that we are ignorant of the men who make the
application, together with the geographical position
of the University, it being remote from us, makes the
case so unfavorable that we recommend the Conven
tion to pass it over without action. The application
from Eochester University, N. Y. ,
we recommend to
the favorable action and Consideration of the Conven
tion. In view of the present prospects of that insti
tution, its geographical position, having direct and
easy access to our several Chapters in New England,
and, above all, in view of the character and scholar
ship of the men who make the application, we ear
nestly hope the Convention wiU see fit to grant them
a charter for establishing a Chapter of the Psi Upsilon
Fraternity in that place. (Signed) E. G. Cobb (P.),
E. W. Thatcher ("P.), J. T. Taylor (A.y, John Peter
son (S-), John C. Holley (B.).'
"
Motion was made by Bro. Taylor (A.), that the
report of the Committee on New Chapters be adopted.
The petition from the University of Eochester for a
charter and the correspondenoe of one of the petition
ers were then read, after which the motion to adopt
the report was carried. Bro. Conkey (F.), then
moved that a committee of three be appointed by the
Chair, who shall proceed to establish the Chapter in
due form when the action of the Convention had been
'
ratified by all the Chapters. To the motion an amend
ment was made by Bro. Taylor {A.), that the said
committee be appointed by the Beta Chapter, to
which the application was made. The amendment
having passed, the motion of Bro. Conkey (P.), as
amended, was carried.
"
The hopes of the petitioners were now in a fair way
to be realized. Nothing was needed but the consent
of the various Chapters. There was no Pi or Upsilon
to interpose its veto, and, before long, all the Chap
ters rendered an affirmative decision, which, we be-
.
lieve, they have never regretted, and for which a
generation of classes in the University of Eochester
is profoundly grateful.
Four classes had graduated since the organization
of the movement for obtaining a charter. Besides
Bro. Barrett,' 54, who has been already mentioned,
only two of those who had graduated from the In
nominata subsequently joined the Fraternity, viz. :
Daniel Bowen, '56, and Melvin Jameson, '56.
CHAPTEE II.
OBGANIZATION OP THE UPSILON.
It will be remembered that the Convention of 1857,
authorized the Beta Chapter to appoint a committee,
who should establish a new Chapter in due form,
when the action of the Convention should be ratified
by all the Chapters. The committee was to consist
of three persons, but it seems only two were ap
pointed, viz.: Theodore Bacon, B., '53, aud Augustus
H. Strong, B., '57. These two brothers, who had
been the influential friends of the petitioners, now
proceeded to make preparations for organizing the
new Chapter. Brother Strong was, at that time a
student in the Theological Seminary of which he is
now the honored head.
The leaders in the matter seem to have proceeded
on the principle of having "the best of everything,
and everything the best," for we find that they ad
mitted only the most desirable members of the In
nominata, and took in several who did not belong to
that society. The Innominata did not long survive.
It had finished its work, and now had nothing to live
for. Those of its members who failed of being elected
to Psi U. were much dissatisfled, but there was noth
ing left for them but "
wailing and gnashing of
teeth," for the Upsilon was to be a select body.
The next step after selecting the members was to
initiate them into the mysteries and joys of Psi
Upsilon. This was done by the committee of the
Beta, Bros. Strong and Bacon, at the Osborn House,
on the evening of February 9, 1858. It is probable
that Bro. Edwin S. Gilbert, P., '55, was present.
Other Psi U's were probably there, but, as I can find
no record of this meeting, it is uncertain who were
present. Fourteen men were initiated, whose names
were as follows : A. 0. Bacon, '58, Egbert Hurd, '58,
Henry L. Morehouse, '58, Ira C. Clark, '59, Joshua
Gaskill, '59, Edward P. Gould, '59, Geo. W. Hough
ton, '59, Sylvanus S. Wilcox, '60, Francis A. Wil
liams, '60, Horace Belden, '61, Henry Cooper, '68,
Charles A. Dewey, '61, George F. Gardner, '61,
Ira Holmes, '61.
John P. Colby, one of the petitioners, was away
teaching at this time and was initiated several weeks
afterward.
After the ceremonies of initiation, a banquet was
indulged in. Dr. Strong relates that the landlord,
supposing a crowd of college fellows would be likely
to "irrigate" pretty freely, had a large supply of
wine and champagne in readiness at the door ; but
when he heard a blessing asked, concluded that
there would be no market for his liquors that evening,
and ordered them carried away immediately. This

<*
C THE
very simple little incident is related to show one
characteristic of the founders of the Chapter. They
were not onlj bright students and congenial com
panions, but also strictly moral young men�
just the
right kind of young men to constitute a Chapter of
Psi Upsilon which should be an honor to the Fra
ternity.
The new Psi U's did not display their badges im
mediately, partly because they wished to get in two
or three more members before "swinging out," and
partly because of a delay in obtaining the badges.
All the Psi U's appeared with their badges for the
flrst time at a Junior Exhibition held some time after
the initiation.
The next step was to give this raw material the
organic form of a Chapter of Psi Upsilon. This was
�accomplished on the evening of February 15tb, 1858.
As the young Chapter had no apartments of its own,
it met in the room occupied by Bro. Hurd, No. 12
Baker's Block. This building is still standing, corner
West Main and Fitzhugh streets. Bros. Bacon and
Strong were present and the latter presided. A full
set of ofiicers was chosen, and a committee appointed
to prepare a code of By-Laws for the Chapter. The
newly fledged Chapter was nowfairly started on its
flight. Whether it should fall, fluttering to the
earth, or, in the spirit of our motto, soar towards the
sun, was
hardly a matter of question. It was
espe
cially in view of the "
character and scholarship
"
of
the men who made the application that the charter
was granted. A Chapter started and sustained by
men of good character and scholarship has no doubt
ful destiny before it.
CHAPTEE III.
PBOM THE OBGANIZATION OP THE UPSILON TO THE
PRESENT TIME.
Beginning with February 15th, 1858, the Upsilon
assembled regularly once a week. The second meet
ing was held in the same place as the flrst, No. 12
Baker's Block. For about two months thereafter the
Chapter met in the "Clinton Hotel, Eoom B," Dur
ing these two months arrangements were made for
renting a Chapter hall, and on the third day of May,
1858, the first meeting was held in the hall of the
Upsilon Chapter.
This room was in a block situated about where
Power's Block now stands. The Chapter occupied
these rooms nearly two years, and then moved into a
room just across the hall from our present rooms.
Afterward the Chapter rented a room in Power's Block,
but, as the boys were not allowed to hold banquets in
the building, they moved into the Martin Block, 59
State street. The Chapter here had the privilege of
occupying the whole of the fourth fioor ; but this ad
vantage was more than balanced by the fact that a
leaky roof permitted the water to disfigure the walls
and ruin the carpets. The Chapter moved into its
present quarters about a year ago.
It will thus be seen that the Upsilon Chapter has
occupied five different sets of rooms. The Ellwanger and Barry Block seems especially favored by the
Chapter. We are now within a few feet of where
many of our predecessors became acquainted with the
mysteries of the order, and it is probable that many
more will here, for the first time, kneel at the altar of
Psi Upsilon.
The Chapter enjoyed the smiles of fortune the very
beginning of its career. It began to initiate new men
before it was a month old, and several new members
were admitted before the end of the college year. The
new society was popular in the University. It had
no difficulty in getting good men, and became at once
a formidable rival to the other societies.
The letters written to the other Chapters during
this period are quite interesting, because of the in
sight they give into the spirit of the young Chapter.
They are full of hope and enthusiasm, and yet dis -
play much of the conservatism which has character
ized the subsequent history of the Chapter. As proof
of this, notice the following passage from a letter to
the Sigma, dated March 20, 1858 :
"Although we number more acting members al
ready than any other society here, we could, I am
sure, increase our number to three times its present
force by practising the loose habits of some societies ;
but, whatever else we
may fail in, we are determined
that "missteps" in the recruiting operations of our
Chapter shall rarely, if ever occur.
"
The same spirit is shown in a letter to the Xi, dated
March 27th, 1858 :
"We have started with the principle to supply the
T. with the best stock, both in 'the material' and 'the
intellectual,' even if, by this policy, we run the hazard
of requiring years to perfect our plans.
"
These musty letters reveal another commendable
feature of both the new
Chapter and the older ones ;
I refer to the warm
brotherly feeling which they man
ifest. The older Chnpters cordially welcomed the T.
into the Fraternity, and the T. replied with hearty
expressions of regard. Indeed, the pages of these
missives fairly glow with fraternal devotion and love.
Of course, the early members of the Chapters w^re
prominent in their classes and the various desirable
positions in the University. This is shown b,y the .
old Interpres Universitatis, the first number of which
was
published in June, 1858, just after the T. was or
ganized. Our modern Interpres would find it diffi-
'
cult, I think, to recognize in this old sheet its inimediate ancestor. Thisisaclear caseof evolutiou. For
a number of the Interpres Universitatis appeared in
the form of a diminutive four-page newspaper. It
contained lists of the members of the faculty, the se
cret societies, the literary societies, (Delphic and

THE DIAMOND. 7
Pithonian,) the various musical organizations, ball
clubs, chess clubs, etc. These lists occupied aU of
the paper excepting two columns, which were fllled
with two editorials of a semi-humorous character.
These old sheets show that the Psi U. boys ranked
well iu college. One of our early Alumni says that,
"although out-dres.sed by one of the competing fra
ternities, out-bragged by another and out-numbered
by a third, the Psi U's regarded their relative posi
tion, in all that makes true society success, with
naught but complacency.
"
It wUl not be out of place in this connection, to
quote from a' recent letter from Bro. J. P. Colby, a
passage which shows clearly the effect of membership
in a
Fraternity upon the early members :
,
'
'The wisdom of our action in organizing a new and
a secret society was attested in numerous ways. A
high standard of scholarship possessed new attrac
tions, now that the society reputation was at stake.
Public efforts were characterized by the college so
ciety critics as
vastly superior to any that we had
made before we
swung out, and we found a sweeter
sympathy, a closer companionship in the secret band
than we had ever known before."
The customs of the Chapter during its childhood
were not essentially different from those now in vogue.
The Chapter began literary work immediately after
organizing. A committee was appointed to examine
all literary productions which were not submitted to
the Chapter as a whole. The essays produced in this
period treated quite largely of abstract subjects. De
bates were frequent. The Upsilon Medley, a Chap
ter paper was read for the flrst time November 1st,
1858, by Dr. W. S. Ely. The Medley was succeeded
by the Protyphon and Excoriator, which are still
flourishing.
The banquets of these early days were furnished
by the families of the members, as Isaac Teall had
not yet made his debut as a fashionable caterer. It
is said that the Kremlin was much patronized by the
*
boys during oyster season and in strawberry time.
The War of the Eebellion was an event of no little

elderly

It was about the time when Judge Finch, as a Yale

"
Smoking Song," that the babe was born in far-off
Norway, which was destined to be a true
"
Child of
song and story.
"
For, if we
may believe the inter
esting account which a Psi U. pen has given in the
pages of Scribner, of Boyeseu's chUdhood, he early
evinced a fondness for tales of adventure and an en
thusiasm for the wild mythology of his native land,
which grew from year to year. Little by little the
resolution formed and strengthened in his mind to
become an author. A partial grandmother praised
his early efforts aud encouraged his early ambition.
It was in vain that his more practical grandfather
showed him that in so poor a country as Norway
literature "could never
repay his devotion with a suffi
cient support. The youth had decided on his career,
and-if readers could not be found in Norway there
were other lands where they might. Thus it was that
in 1869, having graduated from the University of
Christiania, he bade a long farewell to his home and
sailed for America, the promised land of his country
men ever since the hardy Vikings explored the New
England coast long before the birth of Columbus.
On landing in New York the first task which con
fronted him was the necessity of learning the English
language. With this end in view he accepted a posi
tion in an Ohio college, which separated him from
his countrymen and forced him to forego the use of
his mother tongue. How well he succeeded in this
endeavor the readers of "Gunnar," which was written
at this time, can testify. So complete a mastery of
the English language, in so short a time, is without a
parallel in our literature, and caUs to mind the almost
mythical story which Trevelyan tells, of how Macaulay learned German while sailing from India to
London. But we doubt whether even Macaulay
would have cared to risk his reputation by writing a
German history ou arriving in England.

guist and author spread beyond the narrow limits of
the Ohio coUege, and a professorship at CorneU was
tendered him. Entering with his usual enthusiasm
upon the discharge of the duties of this position, he
excited a new interest in the study of the German
poets among the students of that institution. The
character of his work and the thorough manner in
which it was performed, may be observed in his pub
lished volume on Goethe and SchiUer, which is a
memorial of these studies. As a lecturer on German
literature he was
